sources.title: Human History Map, historical-basemaps civilization index and imported border snapshots
sources.note: Project index and six imported topology files checked locally. Both records begin approximately in 1938. Kuwait has seven observed intervals synthesized from six files; its 1938 polygon is a narrow misplaced strip and later polygons exclude a tested Kuwait City point. Qatar is duplicated in world-1938.json and its repeated simplified outline excludes tested points at Al Zubarah, Dukhan, Abu Samra and Al Ruwais. Imported polygons remain unchanged and are not legal boundary surveys.

sources.title: Kuwait Government Online, Kuwait history: Independence and Building the Modern State
sources.note: Official government history checked for the 1899 agreement, education and health councils, 1938 Legislative Council, 19 June 1961 independence, 1962 Constitution and early National Assembly. Its celebratory judgments are not adopted as independent evaluation.

sources.title: Kuwait Oil Company, Brief History of KOC
sources.note: Official company history checked for the 1934 company, commercial Burgan discovery in 1938, first crude shipment in June 1946, later field and export development, and 1975 nationalization.

sources.title: Kuwait Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy, historical overview
sources.note: Official ministry timeline checked for boat-delivered drinking water, storage tanks, the 1952 Shuwaikh steam station and early seawater desalination. It describes infrastructure history, not universal service at every date.

sources.title: U.S. Office of the Historian, Kuwait
sources.note: Official diplomatic history checked for British protection from 1899 and full independence on 19 June 1961. U.S. recognition practice is distinguished from the local history of Kuwait.

sources.title: United Nations Security Council Resolution 660 (1990)
sources.note: Original UN record checked: on 2 August 1990 the Security Council condemned Iraq's invasion and demanded immediate, unconditional withdrawal to positions held on 1 August.

sources.title: United Nations Security Council Resolution 662 (1990)
sources.note: Original UN record checked: on 9 August 1990 the Council declared Iraq's purported annexation of Kuwait null and void and called on states not to recognize it.

sources.title: United Nations Compensation Commission, State of Kuwait environmental awards
sources.note: Official UN Compensation Commission account checked for more than 700 oil-well fires, oil lakes, contaminated groundwater, habitat damage and the funded remediation programme. Project awards are not treated as proof that all cleanup is complete.

sources.title: IMF, Kuwait 2025 Article IV Consultation staff report, February 2026
sources.note: Original 2026 IMF staff report checked for oil dependence, the 2023-2024 contraction, 2025 recovery, reform programme and diversification needs. Forecasts are labeled as forecasts or omitted.

sources.title: Kuwait Investment Authority, history
sources.note: Official institutional history checked for the Kuwait Investment Board founded in London in 1953, its mandate to invest surplus oil revenue, 1965 reorganization and 1976 Future Generations Fund. The authority's first-in-world description is presented as its institutional claim.

sources.title: Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development, timeline
sources.note: Official timeline checked for establishment in December 1961, early loans and continued operations from a temporary United Kingdom office during the 1990 occupation. Selected examples do not evaluate every financed project.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Failaka Island: A Palimpsest of Human Civilizations
sources.note: Kuwait's 2025 UNESCO Tentative List submission checked for roughly four millennia of settlement layers, sixteen archaeological missions since 1958, 1990 evacuation, surviving attachments and threats from erosion, silt and debris. Tentative listing is not World Heritage inscription.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, The Diwaniya, a unifying cultural practice in Kuwait
sources.note: UNESCO's 2025 inscription checked for family, neighbourhood and professional gatherings, etiquette learned by observation, formal and informal forms, and women's growing creation of their own diwaniyas. Practice varies among communities and households.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Traditional weaving of Al Sadu
sources.note: UNESCO's 2025 Kuwait-Qatar-Saudi Arabia inscription checked for Bedouin women's ground-loom weaving, natural fibres, geometric patterns, household transmission and contemporary workshops. It does not imply that every woman or family practises the craft.

sources.title: Kuwait Ministry of Education, history of education
sources.note: Official Arabic ministry history checked for mosque and kuttab learning, the 1911 Mubarakiyah school, merchant arithmetic, handwriting, constitutional Article 40 and later special-education institutions. English renderings in the card are editorial translations.

sources.title: Kuwait statement to the World Health Assembly, Immunization Agenda 2030
sources.note: Original 2024 national statement hosted by WHO checked for vaccination campaigns since the 1960s and the Expanded Programme on Immunization founded in 1974 with free childhood vaccination. It is a government statement, not an independent coverage audit.

sources.title: UNICEF Data, Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Kuwait
sources.note: UNICEF's internationally comparable dashboard checked for 2022 estimates of basic and safely managed drinking water and sanitation and zero open defecation. These national estimates do not establish identical quality in every building.

sources.title: Kuwait Government Online, Amiri order dissolving the National Assembly, 10 May 2024
sources.note: Official Arabic text republished from KUNA checked: dissolution of the National Assembly, suspension of named constitutional provisions for no more than four years, and temporary transfer of Assembly competences to the Amir and Council of Ministers. The page remained live in the September 2026 source check; no official restoration record was located. English wording in the card is an editorial translation.

sources.title: Amiri Diwan of Qatar, History of Qatar
sources.note: Official history checked for the 1916 treaty, its 1935 renewal, oil concession and 1939 strike, wartime pause, collapse of pearling, 1970 institutions and 3 September 1971 independence. Official celebratory language is not adopted as independent evaluation.

sources.title: Qatar National Planning Council, Qatar Atlas history
sources.note: Official national atlas timeline checked for the first crude-oil shipment on 31 December 1949 and first North Field natural-gas production in 1991. It is evidence for dated milestones, not a full social history.

sources.title: U.S. Office of the Historian, Qatar
sources.note: Official diplomatic history checked for Qatar's years as a British protectorate, independence on 3 September 1971 and U.S. recognition on 5 September. Recognition is not the same event as local state formation.

sources.title: Amiri Diwan, Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani
sources.note: Official ruler biography checked for institutional reorganization, education expansion and North Field gas production beginning in 1991. Reserve and superpower rhetoric is omitted.

sources.title: Amiri Diwan, current Arabic Constitution of Qatar
sources.note: Official Arabic constitutional text checked for current Article 1 and the exact sample قطر دولة عربية ذات سيادة مستقلة. The translation is aligned with the official English presentation; Arabic is read right to left.

sources.title: Amiri Diwan, Constitution of the State of Qatar and the 2024 referendum
sources.note: Official constitutional history checked for the 2003 referendum, issuance in 2004, the 5 November 2024 referendum, 90.6 percent approval of valid votes and ratification on 6 November. The government's description of participation is attributed rather than independently evaluated.

sources.title: Amiri Diwan, Amir's speech to the 53rd Shura Council session, 15 October 2024
sources.note: Original official speech checked for the proposed return to appointment of Shura Council members following the 2021 election experiment and the stated rationale. The rationale is the Amir's own political position, not independent analysis.

sources.title: Shura Council of Qatar, History
sources.note: Official current Council history checked for the 2021 composition, the 2024 amendments, Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointing 49 members, their first plenary session on 21 October 2025 and the Council's listed powers. It is an institutional self-description, not an independent evaluation.

sources.title: Shura Council of Qatar, conclusion of the first ordinary session, 6 July 2026
sources.note: Official dated Council news checked only to confirm that the appointed body remained operational through 6 July 2026 and reported concluding its first ordinary session. Members' praise of their work is not adopted as independent evaluation.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Al Zubarah Archaeological Site
sources.note: UNESCO World Heritage record checked for the late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century pearling town, trade links, houses, fishermen's huts, water management, abandonment, preservation under sand and continuing conservation risks. The site predates the modern state.

sources.title: IMF, staff completes 2026 Article IV mission to Qatar
sources.note: Dated February 2026 IMF mission statement checked for LNG expansion, non-hydrocarbon growth, diversification aims and risks including climate stress and possible LNG oversupply. Projections are labeled and not presented as completed outcomes.

sources.title: International Labour Organization, Four years of labour reforms in Qatar
sources.note: ILO's 2022 review checked for job-change reforms, complaints, worker-management committees and remaining implementation gaps, including unpaid wages, retaliation and domestic-worker protections. Figures are dated to the review.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Majlis, a cultural and social space
sources.note: UNESCO's multinational 2015 inscription checked for gathering, hospitality, dispute resolution, oral heritage, women's majlis and children's informal learning by accompanying elders. Practices vary by household and community.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Arabic coffee, a symbol of generosity
sources.note: UNESCO's 2024 multinational inscription checked for preparation, serving elders and guests first, right-hand pouring, cup-shaking to signal completion, poetry and conversation. It is a shared regional practice, not exclusive to Qatar.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Falconry, a living human heritage
sources.note: UNESCO's multinational record checked for training and caring for birds, mentoring within families and clubs, conservation, and Qatar's participation. The practice is shared internationally and not universal among Qatari families.

sources.title: Qatar Ministry of Education and Higher Education, Education in Qatar
sources.note: Official ministry page checked for public and private K-12 systems, differing curricula and nationalities, teacher training and higher education. Its school and enrolment totals are page-era figures and are presented as dated snapshots where used.

sources.title: WHO Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal, implementing essential medicines in Qatar
sources.note: WHO-hosted health-system account checked for primary-care development from 1954 and services including dentistry, pregnancy care, vaccination, pharmacies, laboratories, home visits and referral. Its count of 24 centres is a 2013 snapshot, not current.

sources.title: UNICEF Data, Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Qatar
sources.note: UNICEF's internationally comparable dashboard checked for 2022 estimates: 97 percent safely managed drinking water, 100 percent safely managed sanitation and zero open defecation. National estimates do not prove equal service quality in every building.

sources.title: Qatar NDC 3.0 submitted to the UNFCCC, 2025
sources.note: Qatar's official 2025 climate submission checked for aridity, desalination dependence, climate exposure of coastal water infrastructure, higher treatment costs and possible emissions increases. These are the state's risk assessment and planned responses.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One continuing Kuwaiti polity across a real sovereignty change: late British-protected Kuwait to the independent State of Kuwait on 19 June 1961. Approximate index onset 1938 tracks commercial oil discovery, not founding. Six source topology files yield seven observed intervals through an open-ended 2020-2100 display. The 1938-1945 polygon is a narrow misplaced western strip with bounds about 46.511-47.256 E and 28.854-28.970 N; tested Kuwait City, Al Jahra, Burgan and Al Wafra points all fall outside. Later polygons include tested Al Jahra, Burgan and Al Wafra points but exclude a tested Kuwait City point; Basra remains outside. No alias to Dilmun, Hellenistic Failaka, Iraq or another predecessor. The 1990 occupation and null annexation do not terminate the record. Imported coordinates unchanged.

One continuing Qatari polity across the end of British protection and independence on 3 September 1971. Approximate index onset 1938 precedes the late-1939 oil strike and is not a founding date. Six source topology files yield seven observed intervals through an open-ended 2020-2100 display; world-1938.json contains the identical Qatar feature twice. Repeated polygon bounds are about 50.849-51.605 E and 24.398-26.067 N. A tested Doha point is inside, while tested Al Zubarah, Dukhan, Abu Samra and Al Ruwais points are outside; a tested Manama point is correctly outside. No alias to ancient settlements, Al Zubarah's earlier merchant town, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia or other Gulf polities. Imported coordinates unchanged.
